analysis.one_liner: Requires large warehouse operators to disclose productivity quotas and surveillance data, and guarantee paid rest breaks.
analysis.headline: Introduced and referred to two House committees on August 5, 2025; no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require warehouse employers with more than 200 workers to give employees written descriptions of every productivity quota, how targets are calculated, what discipline can follow a miss, and what surveillance technology tracks them. It would bar quotas that cut into legally required breaks, bathroom use, safety rules, or workers' federal labor rights, and would guarantee one paid 15-minute rest break for every 4 hours worked. Workers could request and dispute the speed data collected on them, and a new Labor Department office, the FTC, and worker lawsuits could enforce the rules with civil penalties. The bill would also direct OSHA to write warehouse ergonomics and prompt-injury-referral standards.
analysis.who_benefits: Warehouse and fulfillment-center workers subject to productivity quotas, a workforce with high injury rates, limited visibility into how their output is measured, and little power to contest discipline based on machine-collected data. Workers gain disclosure of quotas and monitoring, protection from quotas that eat breaks and bathroom time, paid rest breaks, access to their own work-speed data, notice before termination, anti-retaliation protections, and a path to court without forced arbitration.

how_it_helps.text: Covered employers must give each worker a written, plain-language description of every quota, how targets are calculated, what discipline could result, any bonus tied to the quota, and what surveillance technology collects speed data, in the worker's primary language.

Quotas may not prevent legally required meal and rest breaks, bathroom use including travel time, safety compliance, reasonable accommodations, or exercise of rights under the National Labor Relations Act; employers may not discipline a worker for failing a quota that was never disclosed, one based only on ranking against coworkers or the worker's own past performance, or one based on continuously tallying seconds of activity.
Every covered worker gets at least one paid 15-minute rest break for every 4 hours of work, plus notice and posted signs in English, Spanish, and the languages workers speak.

Workers (or a union or worker advocate they designate) can request their own work-speed data and the aggregate data for comparable coworkers in a readable format, add explanations for time off-task such as reporting an injury, and have inaccurate data corrected, with any discipline based on corrected data reconsidered.

Employers must give written notice before terminating a worker and a written comparison of performance to the quota before quota-based discipline, and retaliation within 90 days of protected activity is presumed unlawful unless the employer proves otherwise with clear and convincing evidence.

A new Fairness and Transparency Office in Labor's Wage and Hour Division would investigate, with mandatory on-site inspections when a warehouse employer exceeds 1.5 times the industry injury rate or draws 5 credible complaints in a year; violations carry civil penalties up to $76,987 each ($769,870 for repeat or willful violations), workers can sue with damages of $10,000 to $25,000 per violation, and predispute arbitration agreements cannot be enforced against these claims, with a relaxed path to class actions.

OSHA would have to issue an ergonomics standard for covered warehouse workers within 3 to 4 years and a standard requiring onsite first aid and prompt referral of injured workers to medical care within 1 to 3 years; serious, willful, or repeated OSHA violations would have to be corrected while the employer contests the citation, with stays only for employers showing a strong case that correction poses no safety risk.

The National Labor Relations Act would be amended to make it an unfair labor practice to impose a quota that significantly discourages workers from exercising their rights to organize, with a 90-day presumption of retaliation.

analysis.who_pays: Large warehouse, e-commerce fulfillment, wholesale, and courier employers plus the staffing agencies that supply their floors bear the cost: written quota disclosures and updates, recordkeeping of speed data for years, paid rest breaks, re-engineered quotas that do not measure output in sub-day increments, exposure to per-violation penalties and worker lawsuits, and OSHA ergonomics compliance. Some cost may reach consumers through prices or slower throughput.

drawbacks.text: Coverage is limited: the bill reaches only employers with more than 200 employees across covered warehouse facilities, so workers at smaller warehouses and non-warehouse settings get none of these protections.

The compliance burden is heavy, especially the recordkeeping and data-dispute requirements, and the bar on quotas measured over any period shorter than one day would force large logistics operators to redesign how they manage throughput, costs that could show up in prices or slower operations.
It authorizes appropriations for fiscal years 2025 through 2035 in unspecified sums and stands up a new federal enforcement office, adding federal spending.

The strict penalties, the arbitration ban, and the 90-day retaliation presumption would invite litigation, and an employer that disputes an injury-data trigger for inspection has limited room to challenge it before an investigation opens.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly covered workforce the benefit is concrete: quotas would no longer be secret rules enforced on invisible data, and bathroom breaks, injury reporting, and organizing would stop being quota risks. The costs fall on large warehouse operators and would be partly passed to consumers, and the coverage gap for small warehouses is real. The design is aggressive — sub-day quota measurement is banned outright rather than merely regulated — but the protections target documented problems in the industry: injury rates and quota-driven discipline.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on August 5, 2025 and referred to the Education and Workforce Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee; neither committee has taken it up since, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald Norcross introduced the Warehouse Worker Protection Act on August 5, 2025 with 12 original cosponsors listed at introduction.
The bill was referred the same day to the Committee on Education and Workforce and, in addition, to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, with jurisdiction to be divided by the Speaker.
It has 21 cosponsors, 20 Democrats and 1 Republican (Rep. Lawler).
The full action history shows no further action: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the large warehouse and e-commerce operators that rely on productivity quotas and workplace monitoring: with the bill sitting untouched in two committees, their current practices face no federal disclosure limits, no paid-break mandate, and no OSHA ergonomics standard. Workers at covered facilities remain without the protections the bill would provide.

for.name: Rep. Donald Norcross
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on August 5, 2025 with provisions requiring quota disclosure, paid breaks, data access, and OSHA warehouse standards.

for.name: 20 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Stevens, Magaziner, Boyle, Sherman, Garcia, Norton, Dingell, Ocasio-Cortez, Thanedar, Jayapal, Sanchez, and others)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, the base of support for moving the bill out of committee.

for.name: Rep. Mike Lawler
for.role: Cosponsor, the bill's only Republican supporter
for.what_they_did: Joined as a cosponsor, giving the bill a small bipartisan edge.

for.name: Labor unions and warehouse worker advocacy organizations
for.role: Worker-side groups backing quota transparency for warehouse employees
for.what_they_did: Publicly advocate for warehouse quota-disclosure laws; the bill builds them into enforcement, letting them file complaints on workers' behalf, accompany inspectors, and serve on the advisory board and quota task force.

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral (Chair: Rep. Virginia Foxx, R-NC)
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action since the August 5, 2025 referral — no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action since the August 5, 2025 referral, leaving the bill stalled in two committees at once.

against.name: Business groups such as the U.S. Chamber of Commerce
against.role: Largest trade association of U.S. employers
against.what_they_did: Business coalitions have consistently opposed federal mandates on workplace monitoring and productivity quotas, the same terrain this bill regulates.

sides.party_line_note: 20 of the 21 cosponsors are Democrats; one Republican, Rep. Lawler, joined, and both committees holding the bill have Republican chairs, so the support skews partisan and the bill has not moved.

industries.industry: E-commerce fulfillment and large-scale warehousing (including big-box distribution and courier networks)
industries.note: The bill's covered facilities are defined by NAICS codes for warehousing, wholesale trade, electronic shopping, and express delivery, squarely targeting large quota-driven operations. It forces disclosure of quotas and surveillance, bans quotas measured in sub-day increments, mandates paid rest breaks, and exposes these employers to per-violation penalties and lawsuits without arbitration.

industries.industry: Workplace surveillance and productivity-tracking technology vendors
industries.note: Employers must disclose any third party that supplies or receives worker monitoring data, and may collect speed data only as strictly necessary to check quota compliance. This narrows the market for continuous worker-tracking products in warehouses.

industries.industry: Temporary staffing agencies and labor brokers serving warehouses
industries.note: Staffing firms, independent contractor arrangements, and employee-leasing entities are expressly covered employers, so they face the same disclosure, break, and penalty rules as direct warehouse operators.

industries.industry: Labor unions and worker advocacy organizations
industries.note: The bill gives designated worker representatives the right to file complaints, join inspections, and sit on the advisory board and quota task force, a new formal enforcement role.

industries.industry: Occupational medicine and workplace safety providers
industries.note: The OSHA title requires covered employers to provide board-certified occupational medicine consultation and prompt injury referral, creating demand for occupational health services.

analysis.trajectory: Most bills referred to two committees never reach a markup, and this one has no committee action a full session in, with committee control held by the party whose members mostly did not sign on. Absent attachment to a larger moving vehicle or a change in committee priorities, it is likely to die at the end of the 119th Congress without a vote, though reintroduction in the next Congress is the standard path for bills with organized backing.
